name: Red Fort
label: Red Fort
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lahori Gate' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Lahori Gate' (way/80429907): middle (55 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/264863907: large area 'Red Fort' (1342 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Mughal fortress with red sandstone walls.

text.description:
The Red Fort (Lal Qila) is the great Mughal fortress-palace of Old Delhi, named for its red sandstone walls. Shah Jahan had it built after moving his capital from Agra to Delhi, and it was finished in 1648. The design is credited to Ustad Ahmad Lahori, who also worked on the Taj Mahal. Since 2007 it has been part of a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

The best free photo is of the Lahori Gate, the main entrance. On 15 August 1947 Jawaharlal Nehru raised the Indian flag above it, and the Prime Minister still raises the national flag there every Independence Day. From the approach in front of the gate you can fit the full height of the sandstone gateway, its flanking bastions and the fort's walls into one frame, with sky above. This is the fort's most photographed spot, and the outer walls can be photographed from outside without a ticket.

For a phone, this is a simple, rewarding shot. Stand back far enough to keep the whole gateway in view, switch on the gridlines to keep the walls straight, and tap on the red stone so the exposure suits it rather than the bright sky. Late afternoon light is recommended and warms the stone nicely. Take a few frames in a row and keep the sharpest. The photo spots inside the fort need an entry ticket, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: The Red Fort stands in Old Delhi, the historic walled part of the city. The Lahori Gate is the fort's main entrance, with the approach road in front.
text.directions_text: Head for the Red Fort in Old Delhi and look for the Lahori Gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close to the gate and want its full height and both bastions. Use the default lens (1x) from further back for a more natural look. Use 2x or the telephoto to pick out details of the stonework and the top of the gateway.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (outside, on the approach in front of the main gate). The full height of the red sandstone gateway with its flanking bastions, framed against the sky and the fort's walls. From here the red sandstone gateway rises in full with its bastions on either side, and the fort's walls stretch away to the east behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line the gateway up in the centre, keeping the walls level. Leave a band of sky above the top so the full height shows. For a wider view that keeps the whole front of the monument in the frame, try Netaji Subhash Marg, from across the road.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the red stone to focus, then slide the exposure down a little if the sky is bright, so the sandstone keeps its colour. Hold the phone with both hands and keep it level.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, around golden hour, when the low light warms the red stone.

text.access_note: The outer walls and the approach in front of the gate can be photographed from outside without a ticket. However, access in front of the fort may be closed at sunset and restricted on Independence Day (15 August), and opening times and photography rules can vary, so check the official site on the day.

name: Chandni Chowk
label: Chandni Chowk
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Chandni Chowk' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Chandni Chowk nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/3268564739: the OpenStreetMap point 'Chandni Chowk'.
notes: Busy historic market street of Old Delhi.

text.description: Chandni Chowk is the long, busy market road of Old Delhi, and the best-known frame of it is simply the street itself: shopfronts on both sides, rickshaws and people filling the middle, and the Red Fort's walls closing the view at the far end. The name means "Moonlight Square". The market was laid out in 1650 under Shah Jahan, and his daughter Jahanara is credited with the design. At first it had about 1,560 shops, and the road was around 40 yards wide and 1,520 yards long. A water channel once ran down the middle, and a clock tower later replaced the pool at the square. The centre of the market is still called Ghantaghar. Today the road is crowded and noisy, which is exactly what makes it photograph well. Layers of signs, awnings, wires and faces give a phone photo plenty of depth, and the fort at the end gives the eye somewhere to rest. Stand look towards the Red Fort end, and let the road lead into the picture. If you want a second view, Fatehpuri Masjid at the other end of the road has a white dome with a green finial and red sandstone walls. Keep your phone in a hand or on a wrist strap in the crush, and take a few quick frames rather than stopping in the flow of people.
text.geographic_location: Chandni Chowk is the main market street of Old Delhi. It runs from the Red Fort's Lahori Gate in the east to Fatehpuri Masjid in the west.
text.directions_text: Navigate to Chandni Chowk in Old Delhi using your phone's map. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural view of the road. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the street feels too tight, and try telephoto (2x-3x) to pull the Red Fort closer and stack the shopfronts.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Chandni Chowk (middle of the road, looking toward the Red Fort end). The long, crowded market road running toward the Red Fort's walls, framed by shopfronts and street life. Keep an eye on rickshaws and other traffic, and step to the side when you need to take your time.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the road in the centre, with the vanishing point at the Red Fort end. Keep the shopfronts as even frames on both sides. Wait for a rickshaw or a walker to enter the lower third for scale. For a different view, the dome of Fatehpuri Masjid at the western end is worth a frame in its own right.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the fort or the far end of the street to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Hold still for a moment: Live Photos can capture the movement, and you can pick the best frame afterwards. Wipe the lens first, as street dust is common.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier in the day is usually calmer, and the light is gentler for photos looking down the street. Later the market fills up and the crowds become part of the picture.

text.access_note: The street is an open public road and a working market, but the Red Fort at the far end is a ticketed site, so check the official site before you go if you plan to go inside.

name: India Gate
label: India Gate
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kartavya Path' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Kartavya Path nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/361709652: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'India Gate' (34 m across).
notes: War memorial arch at the end of Kartavya Path.

text.description:
India Gate is a war memorial arch at the eastern end of New Delhi's ceremonial axis. It was designed by Sir Edwin Lutyens and stands 42 metres tall on a low base of red Bharatpur stone. It remembers 74,187 Indian soldiers who died between 1914 and 1921, and the names of around 13,300 British Empire servicemen are also inscribed on it. The foundation stone was laid on 10 February 1921, and the arch was inaugurated on 12 February 1931.

It photographs well because everything around it is symmetrical. The avenue, now called Kartavya Path, runs straight towards the arch, and the lawns and lines of the path lead the eye along it. A phone copes well with this: the whole arch fits in one frame, and the long perspective gives a real sense of scale. Seen from the avenue, the arch is framed against open green lawns and the sky.

Dawn and blue hour are the recommended times for the light. Crowds and vendors are heavy near the arch, especially on public holidays, so wait for a gap or step back and use the avenue's length to keep people small in the frame. Stay on the paths, as the lawns are largely off limits to walking. For a classic straight-on view, you can take it from the paths near the arch, though it is busier there.
text.geographic_location: India Gate is in central New Delhi, at the eastern end of Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath), the ceremonial boulevard that runs towards Rashtrapati Bhavan.
text.directions_text: Walk from Central Secretariat metro station along the boulevard to the India Gate end of Kartavya Path, using the underpasses to cross the roads. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) so the arch and the avenue fit in one frame. Try 2x to bring the arch a little closer without moving. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) when you turn round to take in the whole avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kartavya Path (the India Gate end of the boulevard, looking back west toward Rashtrapati Bhavan). The long ceremonial avenue running away from the arch, with the lawns and symmetry leading the eye along the axis. The arch lies to the east, straight along the avenue. For a second picture, turn round and look west along the boulevard towards Rashtrapati Bhavan, with the lawns and symmetry leading the eye down the avenue.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and put the arch on the centre line, so the avenue's lines lead towards it. Keep the phone level so the arch does not lean. Leave some path and grass in the foreground to show the length of the avenue. If you want a different view, a quieter stretch of the avenue also shows the arch in the distance, with water and grass in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arch to set focus, then slide the exposure down a touch if the sky is washing out. At blue hour, switch on night mode and rest your elbows against your body or a solid surface to keep the phone steady.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dawn and blue hour, per Chasing Hippoz. The light is soft.

text.access_note: India Gate and Kartavya Path are open public areas, but security staff are present, so keep to the paths and avoid sensitive areas; for the Republic Day parade, which uses ticketed positions, check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Lowering the exposure slider helps stop a bright sky washing out in a phone photo.
Gridlines help keep a symmetrical subject level and centred.

name: Lotus Temple
label: Lotus Temple
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Lotus Temple' (1 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/44827278: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Lotus Temple' (99 m across).
notes: Bahá'í House of Worship shaped like a lotus flower.

text.description:
The Lotus Temple, also called the Baháʼí House of Worship, is a white marble building shaped like a half-open lotus flower. It was designed by the architect Fariborz Sahba. Its 27 petals stand in three rings of nine, with the outer petals flaring over the nine doorways and the inner ones curving almost closed around the central hall. The outside petals are clad in white Pentelic marble from Greece. The temple is about 40 metres high and 70 metres across, and it was dedicated on 24 December 1986 and opened to the public on 1 January 1987.

It photographs well because the shape is so clear and the building sits among reflecting pools. The pools give you a mirror image of the petals, and the marble is bright enough to stand out against almost any sky. The classic photo is the full lotus from the front, with the building reflected in the water. For something different, crouch at the edge of the pools and shoot upwards towards the petal clusters. That low angle makes the petals tower overhead, with the marble repeated in the water below.

Photography is welcome in the gardens and outside the building, but not inside the prayer hall. Keep your phone away when you go in, and move quietly, as this is a place of worship. Walk slowly round the pools too, because angled views from the side pathways show the petal structure better than the straight-on view.
text.geographic_location: The Lotus Temple is at Bahapur in south Delhi. The photo spot is in the temple grounds, beside the reflecting pools that surround the building.
text.directions_text: No station is listed for this spot, so head for Bahapur in south Delhi and ask for the Lotus Temple (Baháʼí House of Worship). Once you are inside the grounds, follow the paths towards the pools around the building. The phone icon on the map is right at the temple, at the edge of the water. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the low, upward view, because it fits the tall petals and their reflection into one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for the full lotus with its reflection. If your phone has telephoto (2x-5x), use it for the petal edges and the marble texture.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. From here you look up towards the petal clusters. The photo shows a low, upward view of the petals with the white marble reflected in the water.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Crouch low and hold the phone close to the water's edge, tilting it up so the petals rise from the top of the frame. Switch on gridlines and keep the temple centred so both sides look balanced. For a different shot, walk to the side pathways for angled views that show how the petals overlap, or step back for the full lotus form with the pools in the foreground.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest marble to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the white petals keep their detail. Turn on gridlines to keep the building upright, as tilting the phone upwards can make the sides lean in.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon, when the low sun catches the marble.

text.access_note: This is a Baháʼí place of worship: photography is allowed in the gardens and outside only, not in the prayer hall, so check the official site before you go for opening days, hours and any rules on drones or tripods.

name: Jantar Mantar
label: Jantar Mantar
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Jai Prakash Yantra' (1 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Jai Prakash Yantra' (way/1137558567): middle (14 m across); moved 5 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/223456559: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jantar Mantar Astronomical Observatory, Delhi' (264 m across).

text.description:
Jantar Mantar is an open-air observatory built in the early 18th century, when astronomers worked with the naked eye. Its 13 large instruments were made to track the Sun, Moon and planets. Maharaja Jai Singh II of Jaipur completed it in 1724, and it was the first of the five observatories he built. The name roughly means 'instruments for measuring the harmony of the heavens'.

It photographs well because the instruments are sculptural: curved walls, steep stairs and sharp geometric shadows. The recommended viewpoint is the Jai Prakash Yantra, a pair of hollowed, bowl-shaped hemispheres with markings on their inner surfaces. The surrounding steps give you a slightly raised, top-down view into the bowls, which suits a phone well. Keep the curved markings and the crossing lines in the frame and let the shadows do the work.

For a second picture, look to the Samrat Yantra, the giant triangular sundial. It stands about 70 feet high and is often called the world's largest sundial. Its staircase rising against the sky gives a sense of scale, and a person on the steps helps with that. There is also a second view of its face and slopes from the opposite side, which some visitors find quieter. Please stay off the instruments themselves.
text.geographic_location: Jantar Mantar is in New Delhi. It is an observatory complex of open courtyards and large stone instruments.
text.directions_text: Ask a taxi driver or scooter rider for Jantar Mantar in New Delhi; by taxi or hired scooter is the simplest way. Once inside, head for the Jai Prakash Yantra, the pair of bowl-shaped instruments, which is the recommended viewpoint. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in both bowls and the steps around them. Then switch to the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view of the markings. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for details of the Samrat Yantra's staircase and edges.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject. The paired hemispherical bowl-shaped instruments with their markings, photographed from the steps around them, giving a top-down or elevated view of the complex. The view looks down into the paired hemispheres and their markings, and gives a slightly raised look across the complex.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up a curved rim with one of the lines so the bowls look balanced. Step up a few stairs to see more of the markings. Keep a person at the edge of the frame for scale. For a different shot, the Samrat Yantra's curved walls and steep staircase against the sky work well, or try its face and slopes from the opposite side; some visitors suggest this side for a sunset backdrop and fewer people.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the sunlit stone to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the bright sky and pale walls keep their detail. Take a few frames, as people move through quickly.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon, when the light is soft and the shadows are long.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed monument, so check the official site before you go for entry rules and any photography conditions; tripods may not be allowed and climbing on the instruments is discouraged.

name: Akshardham (Delhi)
label: Akshardham
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Sunset Point – Akshardham' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Sunset Point – Akshardham nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/400921719: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Akshardham' (97 m across).
notes: Elaborately carved modern Hindu temple complex.

text.description:
Swaminarayan Akshardham is a large Hindu temple complex on the banks of the Yamuna, close to the border with Noida. The temple opened on 6 November 2005. It is built from Rajasthani pink sandstone and Italian Carrara marble, stands about 43 metres high and is carved all over with dancers, musicians, animals and plants. It has 234 carved pillars and nine domes, and its base is ringed by 148 life-sized elephants.

The temple is best photographed from this spot as a whole shape rather than in detail. From above the road you look across to the temple, which can appear as a dark silhouette or lit against the sky around sunset. Travel writers recommend this view for that reason, and it is listed as a free photo spot near Akshardham Metro station.

The main temple and exhibition halls are off-limits to cameras, and phones have to be left at the cloakroom. So the view from outside is the one you can reliably photograph. If you do go through the entrance, the approach shows the pink-stone façade and central dome with gardens and water features in front, and Bharat Upavan gives wide garden views with the temple beyond. Check the official site first, as security screening and rules apply.
text.geographic_location: Akshardham is in Delhi, on the banks of the Yamuna, close to the Noida border. The walkover viewpoint is on the highway just north-east of the temple.
text.directions_text: The Delhi Metro's Akshardham station is close to the complex, so start there. The walkover is on the highway, on the left side when facing the temple. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to bring the temple closer across the road, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the whole scene with the sky. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the walkover and traffic in the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Sunset Point – Akshardham (the elevated walkover on the highway, left side when facing the temple; the sources do not give an official name for this spot). The temple silhouetted or lit against the setting sun, seen from above the road. The temple lies to the south-west, and from this height you see it against the sky above the road. The exact spot has no official name, so confirm its location on the map before you go.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and place the temple on one of the vertical lines, leaving plenty of sky above it. Keep the horizon level. Wait for a gap in the traffic if you want a cleaner foreground. If you go through the gate instead, the entrance approach with the gardens and water in front is a good second option.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the bright sky and slide the exposure down to get a clean silhouette, or tap on the temple and lower the exposure slightly to keep the sky colour. After the sun has gone, try night mode and hold your elbows tight against your body so the shot stays sharp.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Around sunset. One guide suggests arriving by about 4:30 PM, so you have time to find a spot on the walkover before the light changes.

text.access_note: The viewpoint is on a public walkover, but the temple campus is a place of worship with security screening and a cloakroom for phones and cameras, so check the official site before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: The sun sets in the west, so from the walkover the temple is roughly towards the evening sun and is likely to look like a silhouette (the exact direction varies with the season).
Traffic on the highway may cause gaps and movement in the foreground of the photo.
Lowering the exposure on a bright sky gives a silhouette on most phones.
Holding your elbows against your body helps keep night-mode shots steady.

name: Connaught Place
label: Connaught Place
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Central Park' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'RWA Central Park' (way/700305761): middle (109 m across).
pin_note: Position from the Wikipedia article 'Connaught Place, New Delhi'.
notes: Colonnaded circular market and business hub.

text.description: Connaught Place is the great white circle of colonnaded buildings at the heart of New Delhi, and it is a good place for a few easy phone photos. Building began in 1929 and finished in 1933. Robert Tor Russell designed it, and the Georgian look is modelled on the Royal Crescent in Bath. The buildings have two floors with an open colonnade below, laid out as an Inner, Middle and Outer Circle, with seven roads running out from a round central park. It is named after Prince Arthur, Duke of Connaught, and was later renamed Rajiv Chowk, though most people still say Connaught Place. It photographs well because the repeating white arches give strong lines and a sense of scale, and the park lets you step back far enough to see them as a ring around you. From the fountain area in Central Park you can take a wide shot of the water and gardens with the lit colonnaded buildings behind. For a second picture, walk to the Inner Circle and shoot along the colonnade as it curves away. Evenings are busy, so a quieter morning suits you better if you want fewer people in the frame. Ask before photographing inside shops.
text.geographic_location: Connaught Place is the central business and shopping circle of New Delhi, in the middle of Lutyens' Delhi. Central Park sits at the very centre of the circle, with the colonnaded buildings around it.
text.directions_text: The easiest way in is by Delhi Metro to Rajiv Chowk, the underground station beneath Connaught Place, then walk up into the circle and head for Central Park at its centre. Once you are in the circle, the park is in the middle, so follow the paths in towards the fountain. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the fountain, the gardens and the curve of buildings in one frame. Use the default lens (1x) for a tidier view of just the fountain with the colonnade behind. Try the telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the arches and columns across the park.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Central Park (central fountain area). A wide shot of the fountain and gardens with the surrounding lit colonnaded buildings behind them.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the fountain on a lower third, with the line of the colonnade across the upper part of the frame. Keep the phone level so the arches do not lean. For a second view, walk to the Inner Circle and shoot along the long colonnade as it recedes. The circular entrance of Rajiv Chowk Metro Station also works as a foreground shape with the colonnade rising behind it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest lit building or the fountain to focus, then lower the exposure slider a little so the lights do not wash out. If the light is fading, switch on night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a railing.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Dusk is a good choice, when the buildings are lit and the sky still has some colour. Early morning is quieter if you want fewer people in your photos. The Inner Circle looks best when the low sun warms the white facades.

text.access_note: Central Park and the colonnades are open public areas, but check the official site before you go for any park access rules, and ask permission before photographing inside shops or doing a professional shoot.
claims_not_in_sources: The central fountain area of Central Park is a good wide-angle spot, with the lit colonnaded buildings visible behind it.
Dusk is a good time for the lit buildings, though advice varies between guides.
The area is busier in the evening, and early morning is quieter.
Low sun warms the white facades of the Inner Circle colonnade.
Photographing inside shops needs the shopkeeper's permission, and professional shoots may need permission in public areas.

name: Humayun's Tomb
label: Humayun's Tomb
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Isa Khan's Tomb' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Isa Khan's Tomb' (node/1754574702): point; moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/2914318: large area 'Humayun's Tomb Complex' (1009 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.
notes: Mughal garden tomb, UNESCO World Heritage Site.

text.description: Humayun's Tomb is the resting place of the Mughal emperor Humayun, and it works as a photo stop because of its layout as much as its size. Empress Bega Begum paid for it. Building ran from 1565 to 1572, and it was the first garden-tomb on the Indian subcontinent. Red sandstone and white marble sit inside a large, formal four-part garden, with straight paths and water channels that lead the eye towards the tomb. It became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1993. Beside the main tomb, smaller monuments line the way in from the west. One of them, Isa Khan's Tomb, was built in 1547, about twenty years before the main tomb. For a calmer picture, start there. It stands in its own walled garden, with an octagonal sandstone mausoleum, carved stone screens and a small mosque on its west side. It is usually quieter than the main axis, so you can take your time over details such as the screens, the arches and the textures of the stone. Then walk on towards the main tomb for the wide garden views and the symmetrical frontage. Keep the phone level and use the gridlines so the straight paths and walls stay square. Check the official site before you go, as this is a managed, ticketed complex.
text.geographic_location: Humayun's Tomb is in Nizamuddin East, Delhi. It lies close to Purana Qila (the Old Fort) and near the Nizamuddin Dargah.
text.directions_text: Use a map app to reach the west entrance of the complex, close to Purana Qila. Go in through the main entrance on the west side. Isa Khan's Tomb is one of the smaller monuments on the way in from the west entrance. From there the main tomb is roughly 400-450 m to the east, a few minutes' walk (this is a rough estimate). The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the garden enclosure and the mosque beside the tomb. Use the default lens (1x) for the whole octagonal mausoleum. Use telephoto/zoom (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the carved screens and the stonework.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Isa Khan's Tomb (northwest of the main monument, inside its own walled char bagh enclosure). The octagonal sandstone mausoleum with carved screens, the mosque on its west side, and the garden in soft morning light.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and line up the octagonal walls so they stay straight. Take one wide shot with the garden in the foreground, then move closer for the carved screens and arches. As an alternative, shoot from the West Gate, where the water channels lead the eye to the main tomb's red sandstone and white marble facade.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the pale marble and sky keep their detail. Keep your phone steady and take a few frames of each shot, as stone detail is easy to blur.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Morning, before the crowds arrive, when the light on Isa Khan's Tomb and its garden is soft. The best light on the main tomb varies by time of day, so take a few shots of it at different times if you can.

text.access_note: This is a ticketed, managed heritage complex, so check the official site before you go for entry rules, opening times and what you may bring.
claims_not_in_sources: The main tomb's facade is best lit in late afternoon, while the eastern side suits morning light (check on the day).
The mausoleum and garden at Isa Khan's Tomb are usually quieter than the main axis early in the day.
The main tomb is roughly 400-450 m east of the stand-here point, a few minutes' walk (a rough estimate).
Tapping to focus and lowering exposure helps keep detail in pale marble against a bright sky.

name: Jama Masjid
label: Jama Masjid
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Meena Bazaar' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Meena Bazaar nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/3926057: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Jama Masjid' (176 m across).
notes: India's largest mosque, in Old Delhi.

text.description:
Jama Masjid is one of the largest mosques in India, and it still holds regular prayers. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan built it at the highest point of his capital, Shahjahanabad, which is now Old Delhi. It was inaugurated on 23 July 1656 and served as the emperors' royal mosque until 1857. Shah Jahan also gave it a poetic name, Masjid-i-Jehan-Numa, usually read as 'mosque that reflects the whole world'. The Red Fort stands across from it.

The photo works because of the contrast: the gateway and domes rise above the stalls, signs and people of a busy street. It tells you at once that this is a working part of the city and not a quiet monument. Put the stalls in the lower part of the frame and let the gateway and domes fill the top.

The lane is crowded, so take a moment to find a gap and keep checking that your phone is secure. The mosque is closed to visitors during prayers, and it is polite not to photograph worshippers without asking. If you go inside, the courtyard gives a very different picture: the whole prayer hall with its arches and domes in one frame. Rules on photography and any climbs can change, so check the official site before you go.
text.geographic_location: Jama Masjid is in Old Delhi, in the old city of Shahjahanabad, across from the Red Fort and close to the busy shopping streets around Chandni Chowk.
text.directions_text: Head for Old Delhi, near Chandni Chowk and the Red Fort, by taxi or hired scooter. Ask to be dropped as close as the traffic allows to the mosque's east gateway. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for a natural street view. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if the lane is too narrow to fit the gateway and domes. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the domes above the stalls.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Meena Bazaar (the lane on the east side, in front of the east gateway). The mosque's gateway and domes rising above the busy bazaar and its stalls in the foreground, a street-level view of the mosque.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Keep the stalls and street life in the lower part of the frame and the gateway and domes above. Turn on gridlines so the gateway stands straight, and hold the phone level, because tilting it up makes the buildings lean. If you want a different view, the courtyard inside shows the whole prayer hall in one frame, if access allows.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gateway to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky and lit stonework don't wash out. In the evening, try night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Evening is suggested, when the food stalls are busy and the mosque is lit. Expect the lane to be crowded then.

text.access_note: Jama Masjid is an active place of worship, so dress modestly, expect it to close to visitors during prayers, and check the official site before you go for current visiting and photography rules.

name: Lodi Gardens
label: Lodhi Garden
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Bara Gumbad' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Bara Gumbad' (way/220693076): middle (68 m across); moved 15 m off buildings.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/80442502: large area 'Lodhi Gardens' (1083 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Lodi Gardens is a 90-acre city park in New Delhi, and Bara Gumbad is its most imposing building. The name means 'big dome'. It is not a tomb but a gateway, built in 1494 in the reign of Sikandar Lodi, and it stands beside a three-domed mosque of the same date. The monuments in the park come from the Sayyid and Lodi dynasties, which ruled Delhi between 1414 and 1526. Little from those years still stands, so the Archaeological Survey of India protects the site. It also works as a photo spot because the heavy stone gateway sits on open lawn with trees all around. You can step back and fit the whole front into the frame without crowding the shot.

Stand on the open lawn and path in front of the monument and face the main gateway. The square, domed gateway and the attached mosque then sit against the park's trees and grass. Early light on the stone is the usual recommendation. In the cooler months, mist can still hang among the trees. Opposite Bara Gumbad is the Shisha Gumbad, a tomb that still has traces of blue tile. It makes a good second shot, beside or across from the larger building. If you want something quieter, walk on to the old Athpula bridge, with greenery and water around it. Locals use the park for morning walks, so expect people on the paths. Wait a moment and they will usually pass out of your frame.
text.geographic_location: Lodi Gardens is in central New Delhi, on Lodi Road between Khan Market and Safdarjung's Tomb. Bara Gumbad stands in the middle of the park.
text.directions_text: Head for Khan Market or Safdarjung's Tomb, the two landmarks on either side of the gardens on Lodi Road, and walk into the park. Follow the paths towards the middle, where Bara Gumbad stands among the park's central monuments. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the gateway and mosque together. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close and the dome is getting cut off. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the Shisha Gumbad's tile remnants or for details of the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject (from the open lawn and path in front of the monument, facing the main gateway). The square, domed gateway and attached mosque framed against the park's trees and lawns.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the gateway up with the central vertical so the walls look straight. Leave some trees and lawn in the frame to show the setting. For a different view, try the Shisha Gumbad, beside or across from Bara Gumbad, or walk to the Athpula bridge for a quieter shot with greenery and water.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the stone wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky does not wash out. Take a few frames, because walkers pass through often.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning, with the light coming from the east. From October to February, mist may still sit among the trees.

text.access_note: Lodi Gardens is a public park protected by the Archaeological Survey of India, and photography for personal use is generally fine, but commercial photography or drones may need permission, so check the official site before you go.

name: Rashtrapati Bhavan
label: Rashtrapati Bhavan
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Kartavya Path' (3 web pages); placed at the stretch of Kartavya Path nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap relation/5354966: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Rashtrapati Bhavan' (271 m across).
notes: Official residence of the President of India.

text.description:
Rashtrapati Bhavan is the official residence of the President of India. It stands on Raisina Hill in New Delhi, at the western end of the great ceremonial avenue. Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker designed it, and it was built between 1912 and 1929. Its first name was the Viceroy's House. With about 200,000 square metres of floor area and 340 rooms, it is the largest official residence of any head of state in the world by floor area.

For a phone photo, the best thing is the setting. Seen from further back along the long, lawn-lined boulevard, the building closes the far end of the avenue, and the avenue's symmetry leads the eye straight to the facade. The road climbs towards the hill, and the slope hides part of the front of the building when you look from the avenue. So expect the dome and upper parts to show best, rather than the whole front. Close to the building, the facade is very large and fills the frame.

This is a secured government area. Stay in the public viewing areas and follow any instructions from security staff. Photography is restricted near the gates on Raisina Hill. The avenue is at its best around sunrise and after sunset, when it is less harsh and the buildings glow against the sky.
text.geographic_location: Rashtrapati Bhavan is on Raisina Hill in central New Delhi, at the western end of the long ceremonial avenue that runs back towards India Gate. The North Block and South Block, the two government buildings, stand on either side in front of it.
text.directions_text: From central New Delhi or the India Gate area, go by taxi or hired scooter to the Kartavya Path stretch on the India Gate side. Walk west along the public part of the avenue towards the building. Keep to the public viewing areas, as access near the gates on Raisina Hill is controlled. The long view with the building closing the far end of the avenue is best from further back along Kartavya Path towards India Gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: From where you stand the building is very close and the facade fills the frame, so start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit more of it in, along with the lawns and sky. Use the default lens (1x) for a tighter view. Switch to telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) only for details such as the dome. For the long avenue view from further back, the default lens (1x) shows the whole avenue leading to the building.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Kartavya Path (stretch on the India Gate side, looking up the axis toward the building). The building closes the far end of the long, lawn-lined ceremonial boulevard, with the axis leading the eye to its facade. Look west and the building is very close, with the facade filling the frame.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and put the avenue's centre line on the middle vertical line, so the symmetry works for you. This works best for the long view from further back along the avenue. Keep the horizon level. Let the lawns and the road make strong lines leading to the building. For a different angle, Janpath shows the building centred between the North Block and the South Block.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to set focus, then slide the exposure down a little so the sky keeps its colour and the facade does not wash out. After sunset, use night mode and hold the phone steady against your body or a wall for a sharper result.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or after sunset, when the broad avenue is at its best.

text.access_note: This is a secured government area, so stay in the public viewing areas, follow security instructions, and check the official site before you go for current access rules.
claims_not_in_sources: Kartavya Path is the avenue formerly known as Rajpath.
Looking west at sunrise, the sun is behind you and lights the facade.
Night mode works better if the phone is held steady against your body or a wall.

name: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib
label: Bangla Sahib
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Ashoka Road' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Ashoka Road nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/839844482: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Sri Bangla Sahib Gurudwara' (354 m across).
notes: Sikh temple with golden dome and sacred pond.

text.description:
Gurdwara Bangla Sahib is a Sikh place of worship in central Delhi, easy to spot by its golden dome and tall flagpole. It began as the bungalow of Raja Jai Singh I of Amber, where the eighth Sikh Guru, Guru Har Krishan, stayed during his time in Delhi. The word 'bangla' comes from that bungalow. It was rebuilt as a small shrine in 1783 by the Sikh general Sardar Baghel Singh. Today it is a place of great reverence for Sikhs. The complex also has a holy pool, the Sarovar, which measures 225 by 235 feet.

From the Ashoka Road side you get the main gate and the entrance facade, a calm and tidy view that makes a change from the more usual photos taken across the water. It suits a phone well because the gate is a strong, simple shape and the dome and flagpole above it give the picture a clear centre. If you want the classic view instead, the Sarovar shows the golden dome and white marble facade reflected in still water, so it is worth a look once you are inside. Photography is not allowed in the prayer hall. Rules around the Sarovar can vary, so check on the day, read the signs and ask a volunteer on site. Please do not photograph worshippers without their permission. Take a few frames from the road, then step back to fit the whole gate in, and check the edges for passing traffic.
text.geographic_location: Gurdwara Bangla Sahib is in central New Delhi, near Connaught Place, on Baba Kharak Singh Marg. The Ashoka Road side is the main gate side of the complex.
text.directions_text: Head for Connaught Place and continue to the gurdwara on Baba Kharak Singh Marg, then walk round to Ashoka Road and the main gate side. It is about 1 minute on foot (about 69 m) south-west of the middle of the complex, so the gurdwara lies to the north-east of it. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to fit the whole gate and facade in from the road. Switch to the default lens (1x) for a more natural-looking view. Use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) for the dome and flagpole above the gate.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Ashoka Road (main gate side of the gurdwara). The gurdwara's main gate and entrance facade seen from the road. From here the photo shows the main gate and entrance facade seen from the road, with the gurdwara lying to the north-east. This is an approximate spot, so move a few steps along the pavement until the gate sits clear of poles and vehicles.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and line up the gate on the centre line so the facade looks balanced. Keep your phone level so the vertical lines do not lean. Include the dome and flagpole above the gate to show which building it is. For an alternative, the Sarovar shows the golden dome and white marble facade reflected in still water. Check the rules on site before you photograph there.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the gate to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little if the sky is washing out the white marble and gold. Use Live Photos only if you want a moving street scene, and hold the phone steady with both hands.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light on the gold and marble. Visit at a quieter time if you want fewer people and vehicles in the frame.

text.access_note: This is an active place of worship: photography is not allowed in the prayer hall, so check the signs and the official site before you go.

name: Laxminarayan Temple
label: Birla Mandir
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Mandir Marg' (2 web pages); placed at the stretch of Mandir Marg nearest the subject (our map tiles).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap node/2833952243: the OpenStreetMap point 'Lakshmi Narayan Temple'.
notes: Large Hindu temple in Nagara style.

text.description: Laxminarayan Temple, widely known as Birla Mandir, is a Hindu temple dedicated to Lakshmi and Vishnu. It was built between 1933 and 1939 by the industrialist Jugal Kishore Birla and opened by Mahatma Gandhi, on the condition that people of all castes could enter. Seen from the street, the front is a tall, layered composition of white marble and red sandstone, topped by three spires, with garden greenery along the foot of it. The highest spire is about 49 m tall, and the temple stands on a high plinth facing east. The whole complex covers roughly 3 hectares, with fountains, gardens and several smaller shrines. That is a lot to photograph, but the street view is the one that fits the whole temple into a single frame. Photography is not allowed inside the temple building, so keep to the exterior and the grounds. If you want a second angle, the temple grounds show the three spires across the garden, with fountains and sculptures in the foreground. Late afternoon or evening is the best time to come, when the marble is said to turn a warm gold.
text.geographic_location: The temple is on Mandir Marg, beside Gole Market in central New Delhi, a little to the west of Connaught Place.
text.directions_text: The temple is on Mandir Marg near Gole Market, to the west of Connaught Place. The nearest metro station is RK Ashram Marg, about 1.5 km away. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the full front. Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) if you are close or the pavement is crowded, and use telephoto (2x-3x) for the spires.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand on Mandir Marg (opposite the temple's main front, looking east toward the entrance). The full front of the three-spired white-marble and red-sandstone temple, with the garden greenery in front of it.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the central spire up with a vertical line. Hold the phone level to stop the spires leaning, and leave a little space above the top spire. For a different view, shoot the spires across the garden from the temple grounds, with the fountains and sculptures in the foreground. Photography is not allowed inside the temple building.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the white marble to focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the stone keeps its detail and the sky does not wash out.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Late afternoon or evening, when the marble turns warm gold according to one blog.

text.access_note: This is a working place of worship, and photography is not allowed inside the temple building, so check the official site and any signs before you go.
claims_not_in_sources: Holding the phone level and using gridlines helps keep tall spires from appearing to lean.
Lowering the exposure slider helps keep detail in bright white marble.

name: Raj Ghat
label: Raj Ghat
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Shanti Van' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Shanti Van' (node/6362111126): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/80429893: large area 'Raj Ghat' (1567 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Raj Ghat is the memorial complex where Mahatma Gandhi was cremated on 31 January 1948. His memorial is a plain black marble platform with an eternal flame at one end, reached by a stone footpath into a walled enclosure. Over the years the complex grew to include memorials to other national leaders, and together they cover a very large area of green space in the middle of Delhi. The name loosely means 'Royal Steps', after the steps that once led up from the Yamuna river.

This stand-here point is in Shanti Van, the tree-lined memorial gardens just north of Raj Ghat. Here you'll find quiet lawns, long lines of trees and the river nearby, which makes a calmer picture than the Gandhi platform itself. Guides often suggest the walk between the two as a gentler photo stop. We can't promise a clear view back to Raj Ghat from here, so treat this as a garden and atmosphere shot. Raj Ghat's own platform, with its flame, lawns and trees, is about 1 km to the south.

Photography rules at the memorial can vary, so check on the day. Keep your phone low-key, don't photograph people who are praying, and don't fly a drone, as they are prohibited. Check the official site before you go for current rules and timings.
text.geographic_location: Raj Ghat is in Central Delhi on the Ring Road, on the west bank of the Yamuna just outside Old Delhi (Shahjahanabad), east of Daryaganj. Shanti Van, where you stand, is in the gardens just to the north.
text.directions_text: Head for Daryaganj or the edge of Old Delhi, then continue east towards the Yamuna and the Ring Road by taxi or hired scooter. Shanti Van lies north of Raj Ghat. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) for the lawns and tree-lined paths. Switch to ultra-wide (0.5x) for sweeping garden views, and use telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out single trees or the river in the distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Shanti Van (north of Raj Ghat, about a five-minute walk). Tree-lined memorial gardens and open lawns with the Yamuna river nearby, a calmer scene than the Gandhi platform itself; the sources do not confirm a direct sightline back to Raj Ghat. Raj Ghat lies to the south, but don't count on seeing it from here.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and use a path or a row of trees as a leading line, with the lawn filling the lower third of the frame. Keep the horizon straight. If you want the river, include a strip of it at the edge rather than centring it. For the main memorial, walk south to Raj Ghat, where the black marble platform and flame are framed by lawns and trees.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the brightest tree or lawn to set focus, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the sky doesn't wash out. Don't use flash. Keep the phone steady against your body or a wall rather than relying on a tripod.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Earlier or later in the day usually gives softer light and fewer people in the gardens, but opening hours vary by season, so check before you go.

text.access_note: This is a memorial site where photography rules can vary, and drones are prohibited, so check the official site before you go.

photo.artist: Humayunn Niaz Ahmed Peerzaada from Mumbai, India

name: Agrasen ki Baoli
label: Agrasen ki Baoli
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Agrasen Ki Baoli' (2 web pages); placed at at the subject (split pin).
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/500411689: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Agrasen ki Baoli' (74 m across).

text.description:
Agrasen ki Baoli is a historic stepwell tucked among the buildings of central Delhi. It is about 60 metres long and 15 metres wide, and a long flight of 108 steps leads down between thick stone walls. Three levels can be seen, and each is lined with arched niches on both sides. Nobody knows for certain who built it. The tradition is that it was built by members of the Aggarwal community in the name of their ancestor Agrasen, and the architecture suggests it was rebuilt in the 14th century, probably in the Tughlaq or Lodi period. A small three-sided mosque stands towards the west.

It photographs well because everything repeats: arches, steps and walls all pull the eye towards one point. That makes it easy to take a tidy, symmetrical picture even on a phone. It has also appeared in several Bollywood films, so you may recognise the view.

The phone icon on the map sits right at the stepwell. The top steps are the busiest part, so for something a little different, walk down to the lower levels and turn round to look up. You should see a bright rectangle of sky framed by dark stone, and a person or an arch makes a good silhouette. Barriers may stop you reaching the very bottom, so be ready to shoot from a higher tier instead.
text.geographic_location: Agrasen ki Baoli is in central New Delhi on Hailey Road, close to Connaught Place and Jantar Mantar.
text.directions_text: Head for Hailey Road, near Connaught Place, which is the best-known area nearby; Jantar Mantar is also close. If you are using a taxi or a navigation app, ask for Agrasen ki Baoli on Hailey Road. Once inside, the phone icon on the map is at the stepwell itself, so just walk down the steps. The phone icon on the map is at the subject itself. The Navigate buttons below take you straight there.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) for the whole staircase, then switch to the default lens (1x) for the shot looking up. If your phone has a telephoto (2x-5x), use it for arches and people at a distance.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand right at the subject: the phone icon on the map marks the spot. Turn round and look back up towards the open sky. You should see a bright rectangle of sky framed by the stone walls, with a person or an arch silhouetted against the light. It is a quieter spot than the crowded upper steps.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Switch on gridlines and line the walls up on either side so the shot looks balanced. For the other classic view, stand at the top of the staircase and let the walls converge into a V-shape. For a portrait, ask someone to sit on the wide steps with the arched walls behind them. Keep the phone steady against a wall rather than using a tripod, as the steps are narrow.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the arch or the person, then drag the exposure slider down a little so the bright sky does not turn pure white. Portrait mode works for a seated figure; for the upward shot, standard photo mode is usually enough.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit when the stepwell is open and fairly quiet, as the steps are easier to photograph without crowds. Bright daylight gives the strongest contrast between the dark walls and the sky.

text.access_note: This is a protected monument, so opening times and any restrictions can change; check the official site before you go.

name: Purana Qila
label: Purana Qila
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Old Fort Lake' (3 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Old Fort Lake' (way/370947967): middle (403 m across); moved 25 m off water.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/973075081: large area 'Purana Qila' (953 m across): previous pin kept, it lies inside.

text.description:
Purana Qila, the Old Fort, is one of the oldest forts in Delhi. The present fort is attributed to Humayun and Sher Shah Suri, who strengthened it and completed its walls, though the exact attribution is disputed. It once formed the inner citadel of the city of Dinpanah. Until the early 20th century it was still known as Pandavon Ka Qila, the Pandavas' fort, because it was linked with the ancient city of Indraprastha. The site is just under a kilometre across, so it is best to choose one view rather than try to capture it all.

The most rewarding photo is from Old Fort Lake, on the lake shore below the walls and outside the main gate. From here the high red walls rise above the water, and trees and grass give you a natural foreground. Guides treat this as the classic postcard angle, and the water suits sunrise or sunset pictures. Turn your phone to landscape first and let the wall fill the top half of the frame, with the water in the lower half.

If you have time to go inside, Humayun Gate is a massive gateway framed by the ramparts and the path leading to it. The 16th-century Qila-i-Kuhna Mosque is also worth a look for its decorative detail. After sunset the fort hosts a daily sound and light show on the history of Delhi's seven cities.
text.geographic_location: Purana Qila stands in Delhi, near the Pragati Maidan exhibition ground. Mathura Road separates it from Dhyanchand Stadium.
text.directions_text: No Underground or tram stop is listed for this spot, so head for the Pragati Maidan area and walk or use local transport to the fort's main gate. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the ultra-wide (0.5x) to take in the full wall and its reflection. Use the default lens (1x) for a cleaner, less stretched view. Try telephoto (2x-5x, depending on your phone) to pick out the battlements and gateway details.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Old Fort Lake (lake shore below the fort's walls, outside the main gate). The fort's high red walls reflected or framed over the water, with greenery in the foreground. The fort lies to the east of you.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on the gridlines and place the horizon along the lower third line so the walls and sky get the most room. Keep a little tree or grass at the edge of the frame for depth. For a second angle, move to Humayun Gate and frame the ramparts and the path leading to it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the brightest part of the wall to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the red stone keeps its colour and the sky does not wash out. On windless mornings try a Live Photo, and pick the stillest frame for the reflection.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Sunrise or sunset, when travel guides say the light on the water works best.

text.access_note: The lake-side viewpoint is listed as free, but entry to the fort itself and its museum may be ticketed or restricted (photos are limited inside the museum), so check the official site before you go.

name: Safdarjung's Tomb
label: Safdarjung's Tomb
camera_source: Researched viewpoint 'Moti Mahal' (2 web pages); placed at OpenStreetMap 'Moti Mahal' (node/10241753222): point.
pin_note: Position from OpenStreetMap way/80950088: the middle of the OpenStreetMap outline 'Safdarjung's Tomb' (554 m across).
notes: Mughal garden tomb of marble and sandstone.

text.description:
Safdarjung's Tomb is a sandstone and marble mausoleum built in 1754 for Safdarjung, Nawab of Awadh and prime minister of the Mughal Empire. It is often described as the last great garden tomb of the Mughals. It follows the same char bagh plan as Humayun's Tomb and the Taj Mahal: the mausoleum stands at the centre of a walled garden split into four squares by wide footpaths and water channels. The garden wall is roughly 280 metres long on each side, and the tomb sits on a podium about 50 metres across.

For a phone photo, the most distinctive view is the quieter one from Moti Mahal, one of the garden pavilions, where the tomb is seen through the pavilion's arches. The arches act as a natural frame, and the picture feels more personal than the straight-on view from the main gate. The red-and-buff stone, the pale marble panels and the elongated dome all show up well against the garden greenery.

If you have time, the gate view is the classic alternative. From there the long channel and garden axis lead the eye to the dome. The back of the mausoleum, with the garden in front, is also worth a look in softer evening light.

Expect some people in the garden, so wait a moment for a gap. Photography may not be allowed inside the main chamber, so plan your pictures for outside.
text.geographic_location: In central New Delhi, at the T junction of Lodi Road and Aurobindo Marg, close to Safdarjung Airport. Moti Mahal is the northern pavilion inside the tomb's walled garden.
text.directions_text: There is no nearby station or tram stop for this spot, so the simplest way is by taxi to the tomb, which stands at the junction of Lodi Road and Aurobindo Marg. The main gate is on the eastern side of the complex. Once inside the garden, head for Moti Mahal, the pavilion on the north side. From there the tomb is to the south, about 2 minutes on foot. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x). Switch to the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if the arches are too close to fit the tomb in, and use 2x if you want a tighter crop on the dome.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand at Moti Mahal. The tomb seen through the arches of the pavilion, giving a framed, more intimate composition.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Use the arch as a frame: step back a little so its edges show on both sides and the tomb sits in the opening. Turn on gridlines to keep the arch and the tomb upright. For a different shot, try the symmetrical view from the main gate, with the long channel leading to the dome, or the rear of the tomb in evening light.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap the tomb to focus, then slide the exposure down slightly so the bright stone is not washed out by the shaded arch. Night mode is of limited use here, because the fountains stay on after dark.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Visit in the softer light of morning or late afternoon. Opening times can vary, so check the official site on the day before planning a sunset visit.

text.access_note: This is a protected monument with a walled garden and may be ticketed, with photography restricted inside the main chamber, so check the official site before you go.

text.description:
Parliament House is where India's Parliament meets, in the Central Vista, the main government district of New Delhi. There are two buildings here. The older sandstone one, the circular building, opened in January 1927 and was designed by Edwin Lutyens and Herbert Baker. The new one stands just to its east. It is triangular, has four floors, and was built to match the old building's height. It was inaugurated on 28 May 2023. On its roof sits a cast sculpture of the national emblem, 6.5 m high.

Vijay Chowk, an open plaza where Rajpath meets Sansad Marg, is the recommended nearby viewpoint. It gives you a wide, uncluttered foreground, and the North and South Blocks of the Secretariat stand close by, so you can fit in several grand buildings at once. Rajpath is a good second spot: from there the building is seen down a long ceremonial boulevard, with lawns, rows of trees and canals on either side.

Photography is not allowed inside the building or the museum, and access around the complex is restricted. Stay on public roads and follow any instructions from security staff.
text.geographic_location: In the Central Vista area of New Delhi, on Rafi Marg, with the new building just east of the old Parliament House and close to the North and South Blocks of the Secretariat.
text.directions_text: The new Parliament House is about 190 m to the north-east of that point. Vijay Chowk, where Rajpath meets Sansad Marg, is the recommended nearby viewpoint. Keep to public roads and footpaths, as access is restricted close to the complex. The Navigate buttons below take you to the subject.

shooting_on_your_phone.phone_lens: Start with the default lens (1x) to frame the building together with its surroundings. Use a telephoto zoom (2x-5x) to pick out details of the building without walking closer. Use the ultra-wide (0.5x) only if you want the whole open plaza at Vijay Chowk and the Secretariat blocks in one shot.
shooting_on_your_phone.where_to_stand: Stand in Vijay Chowk (where Rajpath meets Sansad Marg). Parliament House framed across the open Vijay Chowk plaza, with the North and South Blocks of the Secretariat nearby.
shooting_on_your_phone.how_to_frame: Turn on gridlines and keep the buildings level. At Vijay Chowk, let the plaza fill the lower part of the frame. Keep your phone upright so the horizon stays straight. If you want a different view, Rajpath shows the building down the ceremonial boulevard, with lawns, tree rows and canals leading the eye towards it.
shooting_on_your_phone.phone_settings_tip: Tap on the building to focus, then drag the exposure slider down slightly so the sky does not wash out and the stone keeps its colour. Don't use portrait mode here; it is meant for people, not buildings.
shooting_on_your_phone.best_time: Early morning or late afternoon usually gives softer light and fewer harsh shadows on the plaza, but check what is open and how busy the area is on the day.

text.access_note: Parliament House is a restricted government site, with no photography inside the building or museum, so photograph from public roads and check the official site before you go.
